# Choregos

> Governed agents: workflows carried by agents and people, under budgets and checks you can read.

This file contains all documentation content in a single document following the llmstxt.org standard.

## Choregos

**Choregos runs your team's work through agents and people, under rules you can check.** A request
comes in: an issue, a ticket, a form, a call from another system. Choregos moves it through a
**workflow** you declare. Agents do the steps they are given. People decide where the workflow says a
person decides. Every step has a budget it cannot exceed and leaves evidence you can read. Nothing
moves on because an agent says it is done: the platform checks.

Choregos is open source (Apache 2.0), self-hosted, and works with any agent. It is published by the
Varga Foundation.

### Who it is for

- **A team lead** who wants agents to take a share of the work without losing control of what ships:
  who approved it, what it cost, what it changed.
- **A developer** who files work, follows what an agent does, reviews its result and takes over when
  it gets stuck.
- **An operator or administrator** who connects the tools the team already uses (GitHub, Jira,
  Confluence, Slack, an identity provider), sets the budgets and decides what agents may reach.

It is not tied to software. The same engine carries an HR onboarding, a purchasing request or a data
change: anything that arrives as a request and is done in steps.

### What it is not

- **Not a chat.** Agents work unattended. People step in at the points the workflow names, with a
  deadline.
- **Not a coding agent.** Choregos runs the coding agents you choose, in disposable sandboxes, and
  gives them only what one step needs.
- **Not a promise in a prompt.** A check (a **gate**) is code: tests that really ran, a diff inside the
  allowed paths, the documents a step must produce. A gate that cannot see what it must check refuses.

### A five-minute tour

Here is the life of one request in a classic development project, `billing-api`, created from the
software-delivery template.

1. **A developer opens an issue** on GitHub, "Export invoices as CSV", and labels it `agent-ready`
   and `feature`. That label is the only trigger.
2. **Choregos picks the workflow.** The `feature` label routes it to the `dev-complex` workflow. The
   work item appears on the project's **Board**, in the first column.
3. **An agent triages it**, sizes it (S, M, L or XL) and estimates the risk. **Another agent writes
   the specification**, with criteria that can be checked.
4. **The work item waits for a person.** The specification goes to the product owners. It shows in
   the **Inbox** with a deadline. One of them reads it and presses **Approve**, or **Send back** with
   a reason; the agent then tries again with that reason.
5. **Agents plan, implement, test and document**, on a branch, inside the paths the specification
   allows. After each step a gate checks the result: the tests were really run, no secret was written,
   the diff stays in scope. A failed check sends the work back, a few times at most, then to a person.
6. **Agents review the change**, then the platform opens the pull request. A maintainer approves it
   in Choregos. When the repository's checks are green, the platform merges it.
7. **A release train deploys it**, first to staging, then to production after a release captain
   approves the departure. An agent checks production from measured facts.
8. **Everything stays readable.** The work item's page draws its journey, step by step. Each run shows
   its cost, its evidence, what the agent read, wrote and was refused, and its full log.

Read it in order the first time: what it is, the ideas, a first project, then the daily tasks.

| Section | Read it to |
| :-- | :-- |

| ▸ [Knowledge](use/knowledge.md) | Give agents documents to read: uploads, Confluence, SharePoint, git, the web |
| ▸ [Connectors](use/connectors.md) | Connect the tracker, the repository, the deployment and the other systems |
| ▸ [Budgets and policies](use/budgets-and-policies.md) | Cap what work costs and bound what agents may do |
| ▸ [Assistants](use/assistants.md) | Talk to an assistant, confirm its writes, and keep control of what it remembers and does for you |
| **Build agents** | Write what agents carry |
| ▸ [Skills](build/skills.md) | Package know-how an agent loads |
| ▸ [Agents](build/agents.md) | Create, version and release agents of every kind |
| ▸ [Plugins](build/plugins.md) | Ship templates, agents and connectors as one package |
| ▸ [Tools](build/tools.md) | Give agents tools they cannot misuse |
| ▸ [Assistants](build/assistants.md) | Ship a conversational assistant in a plugin |
| **Integrate** | Reach Choregos from outside |
| ▸ [MCP](integrate/mcp.md) | Connect an AI assistant (Claude, Cursor, VS Code) to Choregos |
| ▸ [Assistants](integrate/assistants.md) | Use an assistant from claude.ai or embed it in your application |
| ▸ [A2A](integrate/a2a.md) | Start and follow a workflow from another agent or an application |
| ▸ [Triggers](integrate/triggers.md) | Start work from a schedule, a webhook or a tracker |
| ▸ [REST API](integrate/rest.md) | Script anything the console does |
| **Command line** | Use the `choregos` command |
| ▸ [Install](cli/install.md) | Install the command on your machine |
| ▸ [Reference](cli/reference.md) | Look up every command and option |
| [Host Choregos](host/index.md) | Deploy, secure and upgrade an instance |
| [Reference](reference/index.md) | The workflow YAML, the errors, the API |

### Editions

This documentation describes the **community edition**: Apache 2.0, one organisation per instance,
everything in this documentation included. An **enterprise edition**, published separately, adds
several organisations on one instance and the identity features that come with them. The console
shows which edition runs under **About**, at the bottom of the sidebar.

### Where the deep detail lives

These pages are written for people who use Choregos. The complete reference, written for the people
who run and extend it, is in the repository: the [reference documentation](https://github.com/VargaFoundation/choregos/blob/v0.26.0/docs/README.md), the
[concepts in depth](https://github.com/VargaFoundation/choregos/blob/v0.26.0/docs/concepts.md), [usage in depth](https://github.com/VargaFoundation/choregos/blob/v0.26.0/docs/usage.md), [security](https://github.com/VargaFoundation/choregos/blob/v0.26.0/docs/security.md) and the
[architecture decisions](https://github.com/VargaFoundation/choregos/blob/v0.26.0/docs/adr/README.md). Where a page and the code disagree, the code is right and
the page is a bug: [report it](https://github.com/VargaFoundation/choregos/issues).

## Concepts

This page explains the ideas behind every screen of Choregos. Read it once before your first
project; come back to it when a word in the console is unclear.

**What you will be able to do**

- Name the objects you meet in the console and say what each one is for.
- Tell who acts at each step of a workflow: an agent, a person or the platform.
- Know what protects a run, what it costs, and where its trace is kept.

### The big picture

```mermaid
flowchart LR
  subgraph org["Organisation"]
    direction LR
    subgraph project["Project billing-api"]
      direction TB
      wi["Work item<br/>Export invoices as CSV"] --> wf["Workflow<br/>states and transitions"]
      wf --> stage["Stage: one transition"]
      stage -->|agent| run["Run<br/>sandbox, budget, token"]
      stage -->|human| decision["Decision<br/>approve, send back, answer"]
      stage -->|system| platform["Platform action<br/>open or merge a pull request"]
      run --> gates["Gates check the evidence"]
      gates -->|pass| wf
    end
    agents["Agents<br/>skills, tools, knowledge"] -.-> run
    connectors["Connectors<br/>GitHub, Jira, Slack"] -.-> project
    policy["Policy and budgets"] -.-> run
  end
  run --> journal["Journal, evidence, cost ledger, audit"]
  decision --> journal
```

A **work item** enters a **project**. The project's **workflow** says which step comes next and who
does it. An agent step is a **run**, checked by **gates**. A person's step is a **decision**. Everything
lands in the journal and the cost ledger.

### Organisation

The organisation is your company or team on a Choregos instance. It holds the projects, the people,
the agents, the skills, the knowledge bases and the connectors that projects share. An organisation
administrator manages it under **Admin**.

The community edition holds one organisation per instance. See [Editions](#editions).

### Project

A project is one stream of work with its own workflows, members, connectors, policy and budgets: a
repository a team develops (`billing-api`), or a business process with no code at all (an employee
onboarding). A project is often born from a **template**, which brings its workflows, its policy and
the agents those workflows name, and sets up the outside systems (labels, a board, webhooks).

A project tells you what it still lacks to run: its **readiness** list, on the first page of its
**Settings**, says what is missing and who can fix it.

### Members and roles

A person belongs to the organisation with a role, and may have a role on a project too. A project role
**adds** to the organisation role; it never takes anything away.

| Role | What it adds |
| :-- | :-- |
| **Viewer** | Read the project: its board, work items, runs and costs |
| **Developer** | Decide the human steps addressed to them, pause, resume, stop or replay work, triage findings, keep personal agents |
| **Release captain** | What a developer does, plus operate release trains and approve a production departure |
| **Project owner** | What a developer does, plus change the project: its settings, connectors, workflows, policy, models, members, its own agents and knowledge bases |
| **Organisation admin** | Everything, in every project: create projects, manage organisation agents, skills, connectors, models, the network and the audit log |

People also carry **groups** from your identity provider (for example `maintainers` or
`product-owners`). A workflow addresses a human step to a group; only a member of that group (or an
organisation administrator, and that override is audited) may answer it.

### Workflow

A workflow is the process a project follows, written as a state machine in YAML:

- **States** are the columns of the board: "To triage", "Specification to approve", "Merged". A state
  of kind `wait` waits for a person. A `terminal` state ends the work item.
- **Transitions** move a work item from one state to the next. Each transition names **who acts**
  (`by`), what it reads and produces (`inputs`, `outputs`), the **gates** that must pass, and what
  happens when it fails (`on_fail`: retry a few times, then escalate to a person).

Who acts on a transition:

| Actor | What it is |
| :-- | :-- |
| `agent` | An agent from the registry does the step, in a sandbox, under a budget |
| `human` | A person of a group decides: approve, send back, answer, or complete a task |
| `system` | The platform does it itself, at no model cost: open the pull request, merge it, open child work items |
| `job` | A fixed command runs in the sandbox, with no model: a backtest, a conversion |
| `decision` | A small model answers typed questions (finished? which team?) to choose the next step |

A workflow is **validated when it is written**, not when a work item is halfway through it: an
unreachable state, a retry that could loop forever or a gate with nothing to check is refused at once.
A workflow is **versioned**: publishing a change creates the next version, and a work item already in
progress finishes on the version it started with. A project may have several workflows; **routing**
rules (by label, by type) choose one for each incoming work item.

### Work item

A work item is one request: an issue on GitHub or GitLab, a Jira ticket, or a request filed in Choregos
itself. It is pinned to one version of one workflow when it starts. Its page shows where it is, what
it waits for, its journey, its cost per stage and what each step produced (its **artifacts**: a
specification, a report, a deck).

### Stage and run

A **stage** is one transition being carried out. When an agent carries it, the stage is a **run**:

- one disposable sandbox and one workspace (a clone of the repository when the agent needs one);
- one short-lived token, valid for that run only;
- one model key, capped at what is left of the budget;
- only the tools, knowledge and network the agent and its project allow.

The runner talks to the agent, records every message in the run's **journal**, applies the guard rails
(allowed paths, forbidden commands, network), and hands the result to the gates. A run that is played
again does not pay twice and does not act twice.

### Gates

A gate is a check the platform runs on what a step produced. It is code, not an instruction to the
agent. A few examples:

| Gate | Passes when |
| :-- | :-- |
| `evidence_present` | the tests were actually run by the platform, not just reported |
| `scope_respected` | the diff stays inside the paths the work item allows |
| `no_secrets` | the change writes no secret |
| `outputs_present` | the step produced every output the transition declares |
| `ci_green` | the pull request's checks are green |
| `docs_updated` | a change to the code also changes the documentation |

**A gate that cannot see what it must check refuses.** A guarantee that passes blindly is worse than
none. The [workflow reference](https://github.com/VargaFoundation/choregos/blob/v0.26.0/docs/concepts.md#gate) lists every gate.

### Agents

An agent is a registered, versioned object of the organisation: its instructions, the model it uses,
its skills, its tools, the knowledge it reads, its limits. Each change publishes a new **version**; a
project runs the version its **production** channel points to, and a new version can be tried on a
**testing** channel first.

An agent has an **owner**: the common catalogue (installed with the platform), the organisation, one
project, or one person. A **personal** agent never runs in a workflow: a process the whole team relies
on must not depend on an agent one person can change or take away.

Agents come in several kinds:

| Kind | What it is |
| :-- | :-- |
| Coding agent | A coding agent the runner ships (Claude Code, OpenCode, Gemini CLI and others), working in the workspace |
| Prompt agent | Instructions, a model, tools and knowledge, with no coding agent: the platform runs the tool loop |
| Voice agent | The same, spoken: a realtime model and a voice, used in sessions, never as a workflow step |
| Hosted agent | Your own container, following a standard contract |
| Code agent | An agent written in code (LangGraph, the OpenAI Agents SDK, plain Python), in an image built from the runner's |
| Remote agent | An agent elsewhere, called over A2A (for example Atlassian Rovo), under the same gates and budget |

See [Agents](build/agents.md) for how to create them.

### Skills

A skill is a folder of know-how an agent loads: how to write a decision record, how your team names
branches, the checklist of a security review. Skills are a library of the organisation, versioned like
agents. **A skill grants no permission**: what an agent may call is decided by its version and its
project, never by a file it reads. See [Skills](build/skills.md).

### Tools and MCP servers

An agent's own tools are those of its coding agent (read a file, run a command). On top of them, the
platform offers:

- **its own tools**, always there: report a finding outside the agent's scope, ask a person a question,
  request a wider scope;
- **catalogue tools**: a short list of third-party APIs and **MCP servers** the organisation chose.
  The platform calls them on the agent's behalf: the agent never holds the credential, never chooses
  the address and never sees the remote tool's real name. A tool the agent may not use answers "not
  found", like a tool that does not exist.

An agent version names the tools it uses; its project can only narrow that list, never widen it. See
[Tools](build/tools.md).

### Knowledge bases and memory

A **knowledge base** is a set of documents a person curates and agents only read: an architecture
framework, policies, runbooks, a product's documentation. Its documents are uploaded or synced from
Confluence, SharePoint, a git repository or a web site, and converted to text. Its **reach** says which
projects' runs are served it; its **grants** say who may change it. See [Knowledge](use/knowledge.md).

**Memory** is different: what agents learn from work, proposed by runs and accepted by people.

### Connectors

A connector is how Choregos talks to an outside system: the **tracker** where requests live (GitHub
Issues, Jira, GitLab, or Choregos itself), the **repository** (GitHub), the **deployment** (Argo CD),
**notifications** (Slack, e-mail), documents, an identity directory. A **connector type** is an entry
of the catalogue; a **connector** is one the organisation or a project has installed and configured.
A project needs only what its workflows read, and its settings say which ones. See
[Connectors](use/connectors.md).

### Human decisions

A workflow names the points where a person decides. Choregos never guesses past them:

- an **approval**: approve, or send back with a reason;
- a **question** an agent asked: answer it, and the work resumes where it stopped;
- a **task** a person does in the real world: fill in a form, attest it was done;
- a **governed action**: a write into another system (create an account, order a laptop), proposed
  by an agent or a workflow and run by the platform only after the people it names approve.

Every human step has a deadline and an escalation. What waits for you is in the **Inbox**. See
[Decisions](use/decisions.md).

### Evidence, journal and audit

Choregos keeps three kinds of trace:

- **Evidence**: what a step measured and left behind: tests run and passed, lint, coverage, diff size,
  and the business **facts** a workflow names. Gates read it; the run page shows it, marked as
  observed by the platform or declared by the agent.
- **The journal** of each run: every message between the runner and the agent, what it read, wrote and
  ran, what it reached on the network, and what was refused.
- **The audit log** of the organisation (**Admin › Audit**): who changed a setting, approved a
  decision, granted a budget top-up, overrode a group.

### Budgets and policies

Every model call is made with a key capped for that run, and lands in a **cost ledger** with its
project, work item, stage and model. A run's key is minted at what is **left**: of its stage budget,
its work item's budget, its project's day and its organisation's month. When the money is spent, the
run stops and a person decides; a stage stopped on budget is never retried on its own.

A project's **policy** bounds what its agents may do: budgets by work item size, the paths no run may
write, forbidden commands, the hosts a run may reach, release trains. An organisation sets a
**ceiling** that every project policy can only tighten. See
[Budgets and policies](use/budgets-and-policies.md).

### Tokens and applications

- A **personal access token** lets you use the API and the command line as yourself. You create it
  under **My account › Access tokens**. Its **scope** limits what it opens: `*` (the API and the CLI),
  `mcp:read` or `mcp:write` (an AI assistant at the MCP door), or `a2a` (the A2A door). An MCP or A2A
  token can be limited to one project. A token is shown once, expires, and can be revoked.
- An **application** (a machine account) is how another system calls Choregos under its own name, not
  a person's. It belongs to one project (**Settings › People › Applications**), has its own daily
  budget, and outlives the person who created it. An application starts work; it never takes a
  decision.

### Editions

- The **community edition** is Apache 2.0 and holds one organisation per instance. Everything in this
  documentation is in it.
- The **enterprise edition** is published separately. It adds several organisations on one instance,
  with the isolation and the identity features they need.

**Admin › Edition** and **About** (at the bottom of the sidebar) say which one runs.

### Go further

- [Get started](get-started.md): try it, then run a first project.
- [Concepts in depth](https://github.com/VargaFoundation/choregos/blob/v0.26.0/docs/concepts.md), the reference page these concepts come from.
- [Where Choregos sits](https://github.com/VargaFoundation/choregos/blob/v0.26.0/docs/positioning.md) against other agent platforms, runtimes and tool brokers.

---

## Get started

This page has two parts. First, try Choregos on your own machine: one command, nothing to configure,
a demo work item waiting for your approval. Then run a real development project end to end: create it
from a template, connect its repository, open an issue, let agents work, approve, merge.

**What you will be able to do**

- Run Choregos locally and approve your first work item.
- Create a development project from the `github-software-delivery` template.
- Send an issue through the workflow and take the decisions it asks of you.

### Part 1: try it on your machine

#### Before you start

- Docker with Compose, and about 2 GB of free memory.
- Git, to fetch the source.
- No model key: without one, agents are simulated and cost nothing. Everything else is real: the
  orchestrator, the database, the gates, the human decision.

#### Steps

1. Fetch the source and start everything:

   ```bash
   git clone https://github.com/VargaFoundation/choregos.git
   cd choregos
   cp .env.example .env
   docker compose up
   ```

   The first start builds the images and pulls the others. Count a few minutes, more on a slow
   connection.

2. Open **http://localhost:3000**. The sign-in page shows a development sign-in with the demo
   administrator, `admin@choregos.local`, already filled in. Press **Enter**.

3. You land on the **demo** project. Open **Board** in the sidebar. One work item, "Plan the team
   offsite", waits in the column **Plan to approve**: an agent has written a plan.

4. Open the work item. The **Decision awaited** card shows what is asked. Read the plan in
   **Artifacts**, then press **Approve**. To see the other path, type a reason and press **Send back**
   instead: the work item goes back to the agent with your reason.

#### What you should see

- After **Approve**, the work item moves to **Approved**, a terminal state, and its **Journey** draws
  each step: the agent's plan, then your decision.
- On the run page (open the agent's step from the journey), the summary says that no model ran. That
  is the simulated mode.

#### What can go wrong

| Symptom | What to do |
| :-- | :-- |
| A port is already in use | Set `CHOREGOS_PORT_WEB` or `CHOREGOS_PORT_API` in `.env`, then start again |
| The console does not answer after several minutes | Run `docker compose ps`: the one-shot services (the migrations, the seed) have exited, every other one is healthy |
| You want real agents | Put an `ANTHROPIC_API_KEY` or `OPENAI_API_KEY` in `.env` and start again; see the [local install in depth](https://github.com/VargaFoundation/choregos/blob/v0.26.0/docs/getting-started.md#fakes-mode-and-a-real-model) |

This install is for a laptop only. With a model key, the workers start agent containers through the
Docker socket, which amounts to root on the machine. To stop everything and delete the data:

```bash
docker compose down -v
```

### Part 2: a real development project

The running example of this documentation: the team behind `acme/billing-api` wants agents to take
features from an issue to production, with a person deciding at the points that matter. They use the
`github-software-delivery` template, which brings three workflows:

| Workflow | For | People who decide |
| :-- | :-- | :-- |
| `dev-simple` | a bug or a small fix (labels `bug`, `fix`, `chore`) | none, unless something goes wrong |
| `study` | a study that ends with one decision record (labels `study`, `adr`, `spike`) | the architects |
| `dev-complex` | a feature (labels `feature`, `epic`, `complex`) | a product owner on the specification, a maintainer on the pull request, a release captain on production |

#### Before you start

- **An instance of Choregos** your organisation runs. To install one, see
  [Host Choregos](host/index.md).
- **The organisation admin role.** Only an organisation administrator creates a project. Ask one if
  you are not.
- **The Choregos GitHub App installed** on the repository's owner. You can do it from the console, on
  the way (step 4).
- **Groups from your identity provider** for the people who decide: `product-owners`, `maintainers`,
  `release-captains` and `architects`. A human step is answered only by a member of its group.
- **A deployment connector** for the release train: Argo CD for real, or the `demo` type for a trial
  where nothing is deployed.
- **Branch protection** on the repository's default branch: required status checks, but no required
  review. People decide in Choregos; the platform merges.

#### 1. Create the project

In the console:

1. Open **Projects** in the sidebar and press **New project**.
2. Under **What does this project deliver?**, choose **Software, from a code repository**. Under
   **Stack template**, choose **GitHub · software delivery (fix, study, feature)**. Press **Next**.
3. Fill in **Identifier (slug)** with `billing-api`, **Display name** with "Billing API",
   **Repository** with `acme/billing-api`, and the **Main language**. Press **Next**.
4. Under **Tracker (where tickets come from)**, choose **GitHub Issues / Projects**. Press **Next**.
5. Check the summary and press **Create and provision**.

Or from the command line, once you are signed in (see [Install the CLI](cli/install.md)):

```bash
choregos login --api-url https://choregos.example.com --token chg_xxx --org acme
choregos projects create billing-api --name "Billing API" --repo https://github.com/acme/billing-api --template github-software-delivery
choregos projects provision billing-api --follow
```

Provisioning creates the routing labels (`bug`, `feature`, `study` and the others) and the webhooks on
the repository, and installs the template's workflows, policy and agents. It is safe to run again: it
resumes where it stopped.

#### 2. Finish the setup with the readiness list

Open the project's **Settings**. The readiness list at the top says what the project still lacks, item
by item, and who can fix each one. Work through it:

1. **Settings › Connections**: the **Source code** card shows "The Choregos App is not installed" until
   the App is there; press **Install on GitHub**, install it on the repository, and come back. Press
   **Test** on each card until it reads **Connected**.
2. On the **Deployment (CD)** card, press **Configure** and choose Argo CD, or `demo` for a trial.
3. **Settings › People**: make sure someone holds the **Project owner** role, and someone the
   **Release captain** role. See [Projects and members](use/projects-and-members.md).
4. **Settings › General**: set the command that proves production is healthy (a `smoke_ok` fact, for
   example a `curl` on the health page). The production check fails without it.

The same list, from the command line (it exits with 1 while something is left to do):

```bash
choregos projects readiness billing-api
```

#### 3. Open the first work item

On GitHub, open an issue on `acme/billing-api`: "Export invoices as CSV", with a description of what
you expect. Add two labels: `feature` (it routes the issue to `dev-complex`) and `agent-ready` (it
starts the work). Nothing starts without `agent-ready`.

Within a minute, the work item appears on the project's **Board**, and the issue gets a status comment
that Choregos keeps up to date.

#### 4. Follow the agents

Open the work item from the board. Its **Journey** shows the workflow as a path: a circle for an agent
step, a circle with a person for a decision, a square for the platform. The current step pulses.

The triager sizes the issue, then the specification writer writes a specification with criteria that
can be checked and the paths the change may touch. Open a step to see its run: its cost, its evidence,
what it read and wrote, and its live journal.

#### 5. Approve the specification

The work item stops in **Specification to approve** and appears in the **Inbox** of the
`product-owners`. As one of them:

1. Open the work item. Read the specification in **Artifacts**.
2. Press **Approve**. Or write what is wrong and press **Send back**: the specification writer starts
   again with your reason.

#### 6. Let it be built, then approve the pull request

Agents plan, implement, test, document and review the change. After each step, gates check the
result: the tests really ran, the diff stays in the allowed paths, no secret was written, the
documentation changed with the code. A failed check sends the work back to the agent a few times, then
to a person.

The platform then opens the pull request, and the work item waits in **Pull request to approve** for
the `maintainers`. Read the diff on GitHub or in the run's **Diff**, then press **Approve** in
Choregos. When the repository's checks are green, the platform merges the pull request and the work
item reaches **Merged**.

#### 7. Release

The release train takes the change to staging, then waits for a release captain to approve the
production departure (see [Decisions](use/decisions.md)). After the release, an agent checks
production from measured facts, and the work item ends in **Verified in production**.

#### What you should see

- On the issue: a status comment with the state, the cost so far and a link to the work item.
- On the work item's page: every step of the journey green, the cost per stage, the artifacts (the
  specification, the plan, the test report, the release notes).
- In **Spend**: what the work item cost, by agent and by model.

#### What can go wrong

| Symptom | Likely cause | What to do |
| :-- | :-- | :-- |
| The issue is labelled but nothing appears | The App is not installed, or the webhook does not reach the instance | **Settings › Connections**: test the cards; a periodic catch-up also picks up labelled issues |
| The work item went to `dev-simple` | The `feature` label was missing | Open the work item and press **Change workflow** |
| "Only its members answer it" when you approve | You are not in the step's group at your last sign-in | Ask your identity provider administrator; an organisation admin can answer instead, and it is audited |
| The work item is in **Needs a human** | A step failed its gates too many times, an agent asked a question, or the budget ran out | Read the step's run, then answer, replay the stage or stop the work item: see [Work items](use/work-items.md) |
| The merge never happens | A required check is red, or the merge queue setting does not match the repository | Read the pull request's checks; set the source code connector's merge queue option to match |

### Go further

- [Concepts](concepts.md), if a word on this page was new.
- [Work items](use/work-items.md) and [Decisions](use/decisions.md), for the daily work.
- [Workflows](use/workflows.md), to change the process the template brought.
- The [template's own page](https://github.com/VargaFoundation/choregos/blob/v0.26.0/templates/github-software-delivery/README.md), for every detail of its
  three workflows.

---

## Assistants

An **assistant** is an agent you talk to. Your organisation installs it for a group of people, and you
find it in the console. It answers from the sources it was given, and says where each answer comes
from. At `acme`, the billing team gives its people a billing assistant that answers questions about
invoices.

**What you will be able to do**

- Find the assistants you may talk to, and start a conversation.
- Read the citations under an answer, and rate it.
- Confirm or refuse a write the assistant proposes.
- See, correct, add to and export what the assistant remembers about you.
- Connect your own accounts, so the assistant reads your data and nobody else's.
- Subscribe to a task, and decide whether it may read for you while you are away.

### Before you start

- You belong to one of the **audience groups** the assistant was installed for. If you do not, the
  assistant is not in your list. Ask an organisation administrator.
- Nothing else. You do not need a project role.

### Find an assistant and talk to it

1. Open **Assistants** in the sidebar. Each card shows the assistant's name, what it does and a badge:
   `ready`, `incomplete` or `suspended`.
2. Press **Converse** on a `ready` assistant. The conversation opens in your personal space: only you
   read it.
3. Type in **Message** and press **Send**. The answer streams in as it is written. Press **Cancel** to
   stop a turn; what the assistant already did stays in the journal.
4. To come back later, open **My conversations** (the page is titled **Conversations**). Each line shows
   the assistant, the number of turns, the cost and the last activity. Open one to continue it, or press
   **Delete** to remove it.

A conversation left alone for a while goes idle. Your next message reopens it with its history.

**What you should see:** the answer, then under it a badge for each document the assistant used, written
as the document's title and version.

#### Citations

The assistant is asked to cite what it uses from its knowledge. The badges under an answer name the
documents. A figure that comes from a source should carry its date. If an answer has neither, ask the
assistant where it comes from, and treat it as unchecked.

#### Thumbs and feedback

Under the last answer, press the thumb up (**Good answer**) or the thumb down (**Bad answer**). A text
box, **A comment (optional)**, opens; press **Send feedback**. A thumb down can become a test case for the
people who maintain the assistant, but it only does so after one of them has read it and decided. Your
comment does not enter a test on its own.

### Confirm a write

An assistant never writes to a source by itself. When it wants to, a card **The assistant wants to act**
appears, with the operation, a summary, the arguments, and, when the source can tell, **What would
change**.

1. Read the card.
2. Press **Confirm** to let it go ahead, or **Refuse**.

Only you, the person who owns the conversation, can decide. The write is made with your identity, and
the source decides whether you are allowed to make it. A proposal that nobody decides within 24 hours
expires.

### What the assistant remembers

From **Assistants**, press **Memory, accounts and tasks** on a card. The **Memory** tab shows one card
per memory space the assistant keeps about you.

- A fact the assistant proposes to remember shows a **proposed** badge. Press **Confirm** to keep it or
  **Reject** to drop it. The same card also appears in the conversation: **The assistant proposes to
  remember**.
- **Pin** keeps a fact in front of the assistant. **Unpin** undoes it. **Delete** removes one fact.
- **Add a fact** (or **Add a profile (JSON)** for a profile space) then **Add** writes something yourself.
  It is active at once. For a space kept per subject, name the subject in **Subject key** first.
- **Export** downloads one space as a file. **Export everything** at the top downloads all of them.
- **Forget all** empties one space, after a confirmation.
- **Erase everything about me**, under the cards, removes every conversation and every remembered fact
  this assistant holds about you, after a confirmation. This cannot be undone.

Each card says who may write to the space, under its name (`writes: agent_proposes`, for example, means
the assistant proposes and you decide).
### Connected accounts

Some sources belong to you: your bank, your mailbox, your brokerage. The assistant reads them only with
an account you connected.

1. Open the **Connected accounts** tab, or the answer's warning **An account is not connected** with its
   **Connect your** (source name) **account** button.
2. You are sent to the source's own page to give your consent. You come back to the console.
3. The account then shows **Connected**, the scopes you gave and when it was last used.

**Revoke** removes the connection at once, and Choregos forgets its secret. **Reconnect** appears when a
source stopped accepting the account. Until you connect, the assistant carries on without that source and
says so; it never reads it with someone else's rights. The same list is at `/me/connected-accounts`.

### Tasks, and the standing delegation

Besides conversations, an assistant may offer **tasks**: work it does for you in the background, like a
morning brief. The **Tasks** tab lists them. The **Inbox** tab holds what they delivered, and your
organisation may also send them by email.

1. Choose how it runs: **On demand**, or **On a schedule** with a cron and your **Time zone**.
2. Press **Subscribe**. **Run now** starts it once, and the result lands in your inbox.
3. **Pause**, **Resume** and **Unsubscribe** stop it as you wish.

#### When a task reads for you while you are away

A task that reads your accounts when you are not there needs a **standing delegation**: your agreement,
for that task only.

1. Under the task, press **Review and agree**. The console lists the exact sources and operations it
   would read.
2. Press **I agree to these reads**.

A delegation is bounded:

- it reads only, never writes;
- it ends after 90 days unless your installation sets less, and you are reminded before; press **Agree
  again** to renew it;
- **Revoke the delegation** ends it at once;
- it is suspended on its own if you leave the audience or if the plugin changes what the task reads: you
  agree again.

:::caution Your organisation may not offer delegated tasks yet
The standing delegation is delivered, but its decision record
([ADR 0137](https://github.com/VargaFoundation/choregos/blob/v0.26.0/docs/adr/0137-a-standing-read-only-delegation.md)) is still **proposed**. An organisation
should not offer delegated tasks until its works council has given its opinion and its data protection
impact assessment is done. If you see no **Review and agree** button, or your administrator tells you
the feature is off, that is why. Tasks that read only public sources, and tasks you run yourself, do
not need a delegation.
:::

### What can go wrong

| What you meet | What it means | What to do |
| --- | --- | --- |
| No assistant in the list | you are outside every audience | ask an organisation administrator to add your group |
| The badge says `incomplete` | a source or a setting is missing; **Converse** is disabled | tell the administrators who own the assistant |
| The badge says `suspended` | its plugin is uninstalled | same |
| **An account is not connected** | the assistant needs your account at a source | press the **Connect** button, then ask again |
| A write card is gone | nobody decided within 24 hours | ask again |
| The last run of a task was refused | it needed a delegation you have not given or that is suspended | **Review and agree**, or **Agree again** |
| A turn is refused before it starts | a budget is spent (the conversation's, yours for the month, or the installation's) | wait for the next month, or ask the owners |

### Go further

- Use the same assistant from claude.ai or Claude Code: [Connect an assistant to your own tools](../integrate/assistants.md).
- Documents an assistant may cite are a [knowledge base](knowledge.md) of its organisation.
- Write an assistant: [Ship an assistant in a plugin](../build/assistants.md).

---

## Budgets and policies

Every model call an agent makes is paid from a budget it cannot exceed, and every run is bounded by its
project's policy: the paths it may not write, the commands it may not run, the hosts it may not reach.
This page shows how to read what work costs, how to set the limits, and what happens when one is
reached.

**What you will be able to do**

- Read what a project, a workflow, an agent or a work item cost.
- Set budgets per work item size, per stage, per day, and for one work item.
- Bound what agents may write, run and reach.
- Know what happens when a budget runs out, and grant more when it is worth it.

### Before you start

- To read costs: any role on the project.
- To change a project's policy: **Project owner**.
- To set the organisation's ceiling: **Organisation admin**.

### See what work costs

- **Spend**, in the organisation's sidebar: **Spend over time**, then the **Top agents**, **Top
  workflows** and **Top work items**, the **Projects**, the spend **By model** and **By tool**, and
  **Knowledge distillations**.
- On a work item: its cost next to its title, and **Cost per stage**.
- On a run: its **Cost**, measured by the platform from the model gateway.
- The **Inbox** lists the **Budgets crossed**: those that reached their alert threshold today.

Model calls and catalogue tool calls land in the same ledger, with their project, work item, stage and
model.

### How a budget works

When a stage starts, Choregos gives its run a model key capped at what is **left**. What is left is the
smallest of:

- the stage's budget (by role and work item size);
- the work item's budget;
- the agent's own run and day budgets;
- what the project may still spend today;
- what the organisation may still spend this month.

Each is counted from what the cost ledger says was already spent, minus the keys still open. Two stages
starting at once cannot both take the same remainder. Below one cent left, the stage does not start.

When the gateway refuses the key because it is spent, the run ends with the reason `budget`. The work
item goes to a person (the workflow's `on_budget_exceeded` state, usually **Needs a human**). A stage
stopped on budget is **never retried on its own**: a retry would mint a fresh key.

### Change a project's policy

1. Open the project's **Settings › Guardrails**.
2. Open **Policy**. Its summary line says the current budget and release trains.
3. Edit the YAML, then press **Save the policy**. The server validates it; an error names the field.

Here is a policy for `billing-api`:

```yaml
apiVersion: choregos/v1
kind: Policy
metadata:
  name: billing-api
  version: 2
  description: "Billing API: modest budgets, no writes to CI or deployment files, a closed network."
budgets:
  ticket_usd: { S: 10, M: 30, L: 80, XL: 160 }
  stage_usd:
    default: { S: 3, M: 8, L: 18, XL: 30 }
    implement: { S: 5, M: 12, L: 25, XL: 45 }
  max_turns: { default: 80, implement: 120 }
  max_minutes: { default: 60, implement: 90 }
  tool_calls_per_run: 30
  daily_project_usd: 150
  alert_at_ratio: 0.8
attempts:
  by_role: { implement: 3 }
  max_stages_per_ticket: 40
scope:
  auto_grant_max_files: 3
  deny_paths: [".choregos/**", ".github/workflows/**", "deploy/**"]
  max_diff_files: 60
  max_diff_lines: 3000
sandbox:
  deny_commands: [kubectl, "terraform apply", "git push --force", sudo]
  network:
    allow_domains: [github.com, pypi.org, files.pythonhosted.org]
    deny_by_default: true
```

What each part does:

| Part | What it bounds |
| :-- | :-- |
| `budgets.ticket_usd` | What one work item may spend, by size (S, M, L, XL) |
| `budgets.stage_usd` | What one stage may spend, by role and size; `default` for the roles not named |
| `max_turns`, `max_minutes` | How long an agent may work, by role |
| `tool_calls_per_run` | How many catalogue tool calls one run may make |
| `daily_project_usd` | What the project may spend in a day, across all its work items |
| `alert_at_ratio` | When a budget shows in the inbox as crossed: here at 80 % |
| `attempts` | How many times a role may retry, and how many agent stages one work item may run in all |
| `scope.deny_paths` | Paths no run may write, whatever the work item allows |
| `scope.auto_grant_max_files` | How many extra files an agent may add to its scope without asking a person |
| `sandbox.deny_commands` | Commands a run may not execute |
| `sandbox.network` | The hosts a run may reach; everything else is closed |

Three presets are a good starting point: `solo`, `team` and `regulated`. A template ships its own.

#### What a policy does not do

A policy does not name who approves. The keys `approvals` and `review.require_human_for_risk` are
accepted but nobody applies them. To make a person approve or review, put a human step in the
**workflow** (see [Workflows](workflows.md)), or an approval on the release train's environment.

### Give one work item its own budget

When you file a work item from the board, set **Budget in USD**. A workflow can also carry a budget of
its own. Either one can only **tighten** the others: a budget wider than the workflow's or the policy's
is refused.

### Grant more money

More money is a decision, and it is recorded. When a work item has spent its budget, **Replay the
stage** is refused unless you grant a top-up. It adds to the work item's budget, and the audit log
records who granted it:

```bash
choregos items action <item-id> rerun_stage --top-up 5
```

### The organisation's ceiling

An organisation admin sets a **ceiling** that every project policy can only tighten: the budgets per
size and per stage, max turns and minutes, tool calls per run, the daily spend of a project, and the
**monthly spend of the organisation**, the one cap that exists only here.

1. Open **Admin › Overview** and find **Policy ceiling**.
2. Fill in the fields you want to cap. An empty field is no cap; the grey figure is what applies when
   nobody sets one.
3. Save.

A project policy above the ceiling is refused when it is saved, and the error names each field. A
policy saved before the ceiling existed is not refused: what runs is brought down to the ceiling, and
**Settings › Guardrails** lists each field that was brought down.

The ceiling's network section bounds the hosts every project and agent may reach, with a deny list that
always wins. **Admin › Network** shows it with the hosts Choregos itself calls.

### What can go wrong

| Message or symptom | What it means |
| :-- | :-- |
| The work item is in **Needs a human** with the reason `budget` | A run spent its key. Read what it did; replay with a top-up, or stop the work item |
| "exceeds the organisation's ceiling" when saving | Lower the field the error names, or ask an organisation admin to raise the ceiling |
| The stage does not start, and no run appears | Less than a cent was left in one of the budgets: the project's day, the organisation's month or the work item |
| A run is refused a host | The host is not in the policy's `sandbox.network`, or the organisation's ceiling denies it |

### Go further

- [Where the money goes](https://github.com/VargaFoundation/choregos/blob/v0.26.0/docs/concepts.md#where-the-money-goes), in depth.
- [Write the policy](https://github.com/VargaFoundation/choregos/blob/v0.26.0/docs/usage.md#4-write-the-policy): every key of the policy and the ceiling.
- [Security](https://github.com/VargaFoundation/choregos/blob/v0.26.0/docs/security.md): what bounds a run, and what is not a wall.

---

## Connectors

A connector is how Choregos talks to a system outside it: the tracker where requests live, the
repository agents change, the tool that deploys, the directory where accounts are created. This page
shows where each kind is set, how to tell that it works, and what to do when it does not.

**What you will be able to do**

- See which connectors a project needs, and why.
- Connect the tracker, the repository and the deployment of a project.
- Declare the organisation's own connectors: a directory, a document store, an MCP server.
- Read a connector's state and test it.

### Before you start

- A project's connectors: **Project owner** on the project.
- The organisation's connectors: **Organisation admin**.
- The address of the system, and a credential for it: a token, an App, a service account. Choregos
  never needs a broad personal token.

### Two levels, three pages

| Page | What is there | Who |
| :-- | :-- | :-- |
| **Settings › Connections**, in a project | The project's delivery tools: the work tracker, the source code, CI pipelines, the deployment (CD), the agent runtime, the model gateway, memory; and **Notifications** | Project owner |
| **Admin › Installed connectors** | The organisation's business systems and MCP servers: a directory, a device fleet, a document store, a web search, any MCP server, and which projects may use each | Organisation admin |
| **Connector types**, in the library | The catalogue: every kind of system Choregos can connect to, and what each one can do | Everyone |

A project needs only what its workflows use. A workflow that opens pull requests needs a source code
connector; a release train needs a deployment connector; an HR workflow with no repository needs
neither. The **Connections** page puts first what is required and missing, and each card says **Why it
is needed**.

### Connect a project's tools

1. Open the project's **Settings › Connections**.
2. On a card, press **Configure** (or **Edit** once it is set). A drawer opens with the form of that
   connector type.
3. Fill in the settings. Type a secret once: it is sealed, never shown again, and can only be replaced.
   Or give a reference to a secret your platform team keeps in its vault.
4. Save. The connector is **tested when it is saved**, and again when you press **Test**.

#### What each card says

| State | Meaning |
| :-- | :-- |
| **Connected** | The last test passed; the card says when |
| **Failing** | The last test failed; the card shows the error |
| **Degraded** | It answers, but not fully |
| **Not tested yet** | Saved before tests ran on save; press **Test** |
| **Demo stand-in** | A simulation: nothing real happens. Good for a trial, not for real work |
| **Provided by the platform** | Your instance supplies it (the agent runtime, the model gateway, memory); nothing to configure |
| **Not connected** | Required by a workflow, and nothing provides it |

A failing test does not refuse the save: the settings are kept, and the card says why it fails.

#### GitHub

Repositories on GitHub are reached through the Choregos GitHub App, never a personal token. When the
App is not installed on the repository's owner, the **Source code** card says so: press **Install on
GitHub**, choose the repository on GitHub, and you come back to Choregos. The installation is found on
its own; there is no number to copy.

For the platform to merge, protect the default branch with required status checks but no required
review, and set the connector's merge queue option to match the repository.

#### Notifications

**Settings › Connections › Notifications** holds the Slack channel and the e-mail addresses the project
notifies: a question waiting, a release departing, a finding of high severity.

### Declare an organisation connector

1. Open **Admin › Installed connectors**.
2. Pick a type in **Add from the library**, or fill in **Declare a connector**: its **Name**, its
   **Type**, its **Secrets and settings**.
3. Under **Available to**, choose **Every project** or **Selected projects**.
4. For each write operation, you may name an **Approver group**: the people who must approve, as a
   governed action, every write an agent proposes through it. A read needs no approval.

MCP servers are declared here too, from **MCP servers** in the library: an official server, one of
your organisation's, or one served by your MCP gateway. Agents then reach them through the platform,
which holds the credential. See [Tools](../build/tools.md) and [MCP](../integrate/mcp.md).

### The network

Choregos calls an outside system from its own servers, and only the hosts your organisation has opened.
When you add a connector, an MCP server or a knowledge source whose host is not open, a **network
access** window lists each host and whether it is allowed. An organisation admin presses **Allow and
continue**; anyone else presses **Ask an administrator**, and the request waits in the admins'
**Inbox**. **Admin › Network** shows the organisation's network in one page.

### How to connect a given system

Each connector type has a step-by-step page: what to create on the other side, the permissions to give,
and the errors you may meet. For example: [GitHub](https://github.com/VargaFoundation/choregos/blob/v0.26.0/docs/procedures/connector.scm.github.md),
[Jira](https://github.com/VargaFoundation/choregos/blob/v0.26.0/docs/procedures/connector.tracker.jira.md), [Argo CD](https://github.com/VargaFoundation/choregos/blob/v0.26.0/docs/procedures/connector.cd.argocd.md),
[Slack](https://github.com/VargaFoundation/choregos/blob/v0.26.0/docs/procedures/connector.notify.slack.md),
[Confluence](https://github.com/VargaFoundation/choregos/blob/v0.26.0/docs/procedures/connector.documents.confluence.md),
[Microsoft Entra ID](https://github.com/VargaFoundation/choregos/blob/v0.26.0/docs/procedures/connector.identity.entra.md). The [full list](https://github.com/VargaFoundation/choregos/blob/v0.26.0/docs/procedures/README.md)
is generated from the platform's own procedures.

### What can go wrong

| Symptom | What to do |
| :-- | :-- |
| A card reads **Failing** | Read the error on the card. A `401` or `403` is the credential or its permissions; a timeout is often the network |
| A card reads **Not connected** | A workflow needs it: press **Configure**, or ask an organisation admin when the readiness list says so |
| "The Choregos App is not installed" on the source code card | Press **Install on GitHub**, then come back |
| A readiness line still says a connector is stale | Its last passing test is older than a week; press **Test** |
| Nothing starts when an issue is labelled | Check the App's recent webhook deliveries on GitHub: the address must be your instance's, and reachable |

### Go further

- [Projects and members](projects-and-members.md): the readiness list.
- [Knowledge](knowledge.md): document sources that sync.
- [Connectors](https://github.com/VargaFoundation/choregos/blob/v0.26.0/docs/usage.md#connectors), in depth.

---

## Decisions

A workflow names the points where a person decides. Choregos never guesses past them: the work item
waits, with a deadline, until someone with the right role and group decides. This page shows where to
find what waits for you and how to answer each kind of request.

**What you will be able to do**

- Find everything that waits for a person, across your projects.
- Approve or send back, answer a question, complete a task.
- Approve a governed action and a production release.
- Know who may decide what, and what happens when nobody does.

### Before you start

- To decide a step of a work item: **Developer** or above on the project, and membership of the group
  the step is addressed to (for example `maintainers`). Groups come from your identity provider, as of
  your last sign-in.
- To approve a production release: **Release captain**.
- To approve a governed action: the role and group its approval rule names, and a recent sign-in.

### Find what waits for you

Open **Inbox** in the sidebar. Its count is the number of things waiting for a person. It has four
parts:

| Card | What waits |
| :-- | :-- |
| **Tickets** | Work items stopped on a person: an approval, a question, a change of scope, a task. Overdue first, then the nearest deadline |
| **Actions to approve** | Governed actions: writes into other systems, waiting for their approvers |
| **Network access** | Requests to open a host for agents, waiting for an organisation admin |
| **Budgets crossed** | Budgets that reached their alert threshold today |

Inside a project, its own **Inbox** shows the same for that project only. You can decide a work item
from the inbox, or open it and use its **Decision awaited** card.

### Approve or send back

1. Open the work item. Read what the step produced in **Artifacts**: the specification, the plan, the
   diff.
2. To accept it, press **Approve**.
3. To refuse it, type what is wrong in **Reason for sending back** and press **Send back**. The workflow
   goes where it says on a rejection, usually back to the agent, which receives your reason.

From the command line:

```bash
choregos items approve <item-id>
choregos items reject <item-id> --reason "The export must include credit notes."
```

### Answer a question

When an agent is blocked, it does not guess: it asks. The work item moves to a waiting state (often
**Needs a human**) and the people of the step's group are notified.

1. Open the work item. The question is in **Decision awaited**.
2. Type your reply in **Answer** and press **Answer**.

The agent's stage resumes where it stopped, with your answer and one more attempt.

```bash
choregos items answer <item-id> "Use the customer's billing currency."
```

### Accept or refuse a change of scope

An agent that needs to touch a path outside its allowed scope asks for it. A small request (a few
files, as the project's policy allows) is granted on its own. A larger one waits for a person: press
**Approve** to widen the scope for this work item, or **Send back** with a reason.

### Complete a task

Some steps are done by a person in the real world: hand over a badge, set up a workstation, sign a
contract. The step shows a form and, often, a sentence to attest.

1. Open the work item. The task's instructions are in **Decision awaited**.
2. Fill in the form. Required fields are listed under "To fill" until they are filled.
3. If the task asks for it, tick **I attest** and the sentence it shows.
4. Press **Done**. The values become fields of the work item, and the next step reads them.

If the task cannot be done, write why in **Why it cannot be done** and press **Cannot do it**.

### Approve a governed action

A write into a system that is not Choregos (create an account, order a laptop, deactivate a badge) is a
**governed action**. An agent or a workflow proposes it; the people its approval rule names decide; then
the platform runs it, step by step, and undoes what it did if a step fails.

1. Open **Inbox**, then the action under **Actions to approve**. Its page lists what it will do, effect
   by effect, and with which parameters.
2. Press **Approve**, or write a **Reason to reject** and press **Reject**.

Three rules apply:

- **A recent sign-in.** An approval rule may require that you signed in a few minutes ago. If you did
  not, the console sends you through your identity provider again, then brings you back.
- **Not your own proposal.** The person who proposed the action, or who owns the agent that proposed
  it, does not decide it.
- **Several approvers.** A rule may ask for two different people.

The action's page then shows its journal: every effect, its attempts, its answer or its error.

### Approve a production release

A release train batches what is ready and deploys it. When the project's policy or the workflow asks
for an approval before production:

1. Open the project's **Trains**.
2. Find the batch waiting for approval and press **Approve**. The confirmation names the batch and how
   many work items it carries.

```bash
choregos trains status billing-api
choregos trains approve <release-id> --note "Checked with support"
```

### Deadlines and escalations

Every human step can carry a deadline (`sla_hours` on the group, `timeout_hours` on the transition).
The inbox puts overdue requests first. When a step times out, the work item goes where its workflow
says, usually **Needs a human**, and from there a person decides to resume or abandon it.

### Who decides when nobody can

A step addressed to a group that nobody carries would wait forever. An **organisation admin** may answer
any step; doing so outside the group is recorded in the audit log as an override, with the group it
bypassed.

### Decisions stay in the console

A `/choregos approve`, `reject` or `answer` comment on an issue does not decide anything. Choregos
replies on the issue with a link to the inbox. A decision is taken by a signed-in person, in the
console or with their own token.

### What can go wrong

| Message | What it means |
| :-- | :-- |
| "deciding needs at least the developer role" | You are a viewer on this project |
| "this step is addressed to the group … only its members answer it" | You do not carry the step's group at your last sign-in; sign in again after your identity provider adds you, or ask an organisation admin |
| "no human request is pending on this work item" | Someone decided before you, or the work item moved on |
| "approving a release needs the release_captain role" | Ask a project owner for the role |

### Go further

- [Work items](work-items.md): what happens after your decision.
- [Workflows](workflows.md): where a workflow names who decides.
- [Governed actions](https://github.com/VargaFoundation/choregos/blob/v0.26.0/docs/usage.md#4-bis-governed-actions), in depth.

---

## Knowledge

A knowledge base is a set of documents a person curates and agents only read: an architecture
framework, security rules, runbooks, a product's documentation, a few decks and spreadsheets. This page
shows how to create one, feed it, keep it current, and decide who uses it.

**What you will be able to do**

- Create a knowledge base for one project, or for the whole organisation.
- Feed it with uploads and with sources that sync on their own.
- Choose how runs read it: as files, or as a searchable index.
- Decide which runs are served it and who may change it.
- Keep a knowledge base as code, in a file you review.

### Before you start

- For a project's own knowledge base: **Project owner** on that project.
- For an organisation-wide knowledge base, or one shared by several projects: **Organisation admin**.
- To sync from Confluence or SharePoint: a connector of that kind, declared by an organisation admin
  (see [Connectors](connectors.md)).

An [assistant](assistants.md) reads the knowledge bases its plugin seeded, and cites the documents it
uses.

### Knowledge or memory?

| | Knowledge base | Memory |
| :-- | :-- | :-- |
| Holds | Documents a person chose | What agents learnt from work |
| Written by | People: uploads and synced sources | Runs propose, people accept |
| Agents | Read only | Read, and propose |

For a handful of facts only one work item needs, give the document as an input of the work item
instead of keeping a base that must be synced.

### Create a knowledge base

#### For one project

1. Open the project, then **Knowledge** in the sidebar. It lists the project's own bases, then those
   shared with every project.
2. Press **New knowledge base**, give it a name, and create it. It is served to this project's runs
   only, and the project's owners curate it.

#### For the organisation

1. Open **Knowledge** in the organisation's sidebar. It lists every base, with who uses each one.
2. In **Create a knowledge base**, choose who it is for: the whole organisation, a list of projects, or
   the people of some identity-provider groups (a group's base is for people, never for a run).

### Feed it

Open the base. Its status banner says whether it can be used now: **Ready**, or still converting or
syncing, with a progress bar.

- **Upload documents**: Word, PowerPoint, Excel, PDF, HTML, Markdown, text, YAML, JSON, TOML, up to
  20 MiB each by default. Each file is converted to text in the background; uploading a file with the
  same name replaces it.
- **Add a source** that syncs on a schedule: a **Confluence space or page tree**, **SharePoint /
  OneDrive**, a **git repository** or a **web site**. For a web source, tick **This page only (no links
  followed)** for one address, and **Include linked documents (PDF, Word, PowerPoint, Excel)** to read
  the files it links to.

Each source shows when it last synced, what it added, updated, deleted or skipped, and its last error.
A document deleted at the source leaves the base at the next sync.

What conversion keeps: headings, slide titles and speaker notes, tables, each sheet of a workbook as a
table with the values Excel last saved. What it loses: **images and charts are not described**, and
there is **no OCR**, so a scanned PDF fails.

### Choose how runs read it

On the base's page, the **How runs read it** card sets the **Serving mode**:

| Mode | How it works | Use it when |
| :-- | :-- | :-- |
| Files | The ready documents are laid read-only in the run's workspace; the agent reads them like any file | The text fits in a model's context: up to roughly 200,000 tokens |
| Index | The documents are cut into passages; the agent searches them and cites what it used | The base is larger, or you want citations |

To check an index, write a few questions with the documents expected to answer them (the **Eval set**)
and run it.

### Let an agent read it

A base is read by the agents that name it, in runs of the projects it is served to. The base's
**Who uses it** card lists the **Agents that read it** and the **Runs it may be served to**. To add one,
name the base in the agent's knowledge (see [Agents](../build/agents.md)). A run whose project is not
served a base its agent names does not start, and says why.

### Decide who may change it

Reach decides which runs are served a base. **Grants** decide which people may change it. On the
base's **Access** card, give a member, a group or a project's members a role:

| Gesture | Viewer | Editor | Owner | Organisation admin, or owner of the owning project |
| :-- | :-- | :-- | :-- | :-- |
| Read | yes | yes | yes | yes |
| Upload, add a source, sync, distil, rename | no | yes | yes | yes |
| Share, archive | no | no | yes | yes |
| Widen who it is served to, restrict it | no | no | no | yes |

A **restricted** base is read by people only through a grant, and served to a run only on behalf of
the person who started the work item. A work item started by a schedule or a tracker names no person,
so its runs stop before they start. What such a run writes stays visible only to the base's readers.

A sync from Confluence or SharePoint reads with a service account: everything that account can read
in the chosen space becomes readable by the base's readers. Give that account access to what you mean
to share, and nothing else.

### Turn a base into a skill

A base can be **distilled** into a skill of short principles, each citing the document it came from.
The page first shows an estimate (documents, model calls, cost) with no model call; you can leave the
biggest documents out. The distilled skill waits for an administrator's review before any agent
carries it.

### Keep a knowledge base as code

A manifest describes a base, its sources, its uploads and its eval set. Applying it makes the base
match the file; applying it again changes nothing.

```yaml
apiVersion: choregos/v1
kind: KnowledgeBase
slug: billing-docs
name: Billing documentation
description: The product's documentation and the finance team's rules, for the billing agents.
scope: projects
projects: [billing-api]
serving_mode: index
sources:
  - name: handbook
    kind: git
    config:
      url: https://github.com/acme/handbook.git
      ref: main
      paths: ["docs/**/*.md"]
    interval_minutes: 60
  - name: public-pricing
    kind: web
    config:
      url: https://acme.example/pricing
      max_depth: 1
    interval_minutes: 1440
uploads:
  - finance/*.xlsx
eval:
  - question: How is a credit note numbered?
    expected: [numbering.md]
```

```bash
choregos knowledge apply -f billing-docs.yaml --dry-run
choregos knowledge apply -f billing-docs.yaml
choregos knowledge sync billing-docs
choregos knowledge eval billing-docs
```

`--dry-run` prints the plan and changes nothing. Without `--prune`, sources and uploads the file does
not list are left alone. These commands need an organisation admin's token.

### What can go wrong

| Symptom | What to do |
| :-- | :-- |
| A document reads **Failed** | Read its reason: a scanned PDF, a file too large, a format the converter does not read. Fix the file and upload it again |
| A source cannot be added: the host is not allowed | The organisation must open that host for its network. An admin presses **Allow and continue**; anyone else presses **Ask an administrator** |
| A Confluence or SharePoint source cannot sync | The organisation has no connector of that kind yet; ask an organisation admin |
| A run stops before it starts and names a knowledge base | The run's project is not served that base, or the base is restricted and the work item names no person who reads it |

### Go further

- [Knowledge bases](https://github.com/VargaFoundation/choregos/blob/v0.26.0/docs/usage.md#knowledge-bases), in depth: conversion, sources, distillation.
- [Skills](../build/skills.md): what a distilled base becomes.

---

## Projects and members

A project is where a team's work runs: its workflows, its connectors, its policy, its people. This
page shows how to create one and who can do what in it.

**What you will be able to do**

- Create a project, with or without a template, with or without a code repository.
- Read the readiness list and fix what the project still lacks.
- Invite people and give them a role on the organisation or on one project.
- Give an application its own account on a project.

### Before you start

- To create a project: the **Organisation admin** role.
- To invite people to a project or change its settings: the **Project owner** role on it.

### Create a project

#### From the console

1. Open **Projects** in the sidebar and press **New project**.
2. Answer **What does this project deliver?**:
   - **Software, from a code repository**: agents plan, change and deliver the code of a repository.
     Pick a **Stack template**, or **None — I wire my connectors myself**.
   - **A business process, no code repository**: HR onboarding, purchasing, legal, support. Pick a
     **Workflow** from the library; it becomes the project's default.
3. **Identifier (slug)**: lowercase letters, digits and dashes, for example `billing-api`. It is in
   every address and cannot be changed later. **Display name**: what people read.
4. For software: the **Repository** (`owner/name` or an https address) and the **Main language**.
5. **Tracker (where tickets come from)**: **Choregos (requests are filed here)**, **GitHub Issues /
   Projects**, **Jira** or **GitLab**. A Slack channel for notifications is optional.
6. Read the summary and press **Create and provision** (with a template) or **Create**.

If a step fails half-way, the wizard keeps what was already created: press **Retry**, and it goes on
from there.

#### From the command line

```bash
choregos projects create billing-api --name "Billing API" --repo https://github.com/acme/billing-api --template github-software-delivery
choregos projects provision billing-api --follow
```

A project without a repository files its requests in Choregos itself:

```bash
choregos projects create onboarding --name "Employee onboarding"
```

#### Which template

| Template | When |
| :-- | :-- |
| `github-software-delivery` | A software team on GitHub Actions: fixes, studies that end in a decision record, features with three human approvals |
| `software-delivery-governed` | Changes that must pass everything: an approved decision record, mutation testing, security and compliance reviews decided by people |
| `github-tekton-argo-k8s` | You run your own CI (Tekton) and deployment (Argo CD) on Kubernetes |
| `github-aca` | You are on Azure and run agents as Container Apps jobs |
| `joiners-leavers` | HR arrivals and departures, with no repository; every write into another system is approved |
| none | You attach the connectors and the workflow yourself |

A template brings the workflows, the policy and the agents those workflows name. Agents enter the
organisation the first time a project is born from the template; an agent the organisation already
has is never overwritten.

### Check what the project still lacks

Open the project's **Settings**. The first page shows the **readiness** list: one line per thing the
project needs, its state, and who can fix it.

| State | Meaning |
| :-- | :-- |
| Done | Configured and working |
| To check | It works, but deserves a look: a demo stand-in, a connector not tested for a week |
| To do | The project cannot run as intended until this is fixed |
| Not needed | No workflow of the project uses it |

The card's header sums it up: **Ready to run**, or how many lines are left to do.

Each open line has a **Fix** link to the page that fixes it. When you cannot fix it yourself, the line
says whom to ask: a project owner, the organisation admin, the platform operator, or someone outside
Choregos (your identity provider, a vendor). The project's **Overview** shows the same list as a
**Getting started** card until nothing is left to do.

```bash
choregos projects readiness billing-api
```

The readiness list is read from what is stored: the last connector tests, the policy, the members, the
workflows. It does not call the outside systems. Press **Test** on a connector to refresh it.

### The settings, group by group

| Group | What it holds |
| :-- | :-- |
| **General** | Name, status, repository, the commands that prove the work (tests, lint, type checks) and the facts that prove production is healthy |
| **Connections** | The tracker, the repository, the deployment, the agent runtime; notifications |
| **Agents** | The backend and models agents run on, the tools they may call, A2A, knowledge and memory |
| **Guardrails** | The policy, and the hosts a run may reach |
| **People** | Who works on the project, and the applications that call it |
| **Danger zone** | Suspend or archive the project |

Each section saves on its own. If someone else saved the same settings in between, the console reads
them again and merges; if it cannot, it asks you to reload the page.

### Invite people and give them roles

Roles go from least to most: **Viewer**, **Developer**, **Release captain**, **Project owner**,
**Organisation admin**. See [Members and roles](../concepts.md#members-and-roles) for what each one
adds.

#### On one project

1. Open the project, then **Members** in the sidebar.
2. In **Members of this project**, type the person's **Member e-mail**, pick the **Role**, and press
   **Invite**.

#### On the whole organisation

1. Open **Admin › Members**.
2. Type the **Member e-mail**, choose the **Scope**: **The whole organisation** or one project, pick
   the **Role**, and press **Invite**.

A project role **adds** to the organisation role: someone who is a developer of the organisation is
at least a developer on every project. To give someone less on one project, give them less on the
organisation.

#### Groups

People also carry groups from your identity provider, read at each sign-in. Workflows address their
human steps to groups (`maintainers`, `product-owners`). The readiness list warns when a workflow names
a group that nobody has ever carried at sign-in. Groups are managed in your identity provider, not in
Choregos; when your provider withdraws a role it granted, Choregos removes it at the person's next
sign-in.

### Give an application its own account

When another system starts work in a project (a portal, a script, another agent), give it an
**application** rather than a person's token. It acts under its own name, has its own daily budget,
and keeps working when the person who created it leaves.

1. Open **Settings › People**. In the **Applications** card, type a short name under **New
   application** (lowercase letters, digits and hyphens) and press **Create**.
2. Press **Issue a token** on its line. The token is shown **once**: copy it into the calling
   system's secret store.

```bash
choregos machines create billing-api invoicing-portal --display-name "Invoicing portal"
choregos machines token billing-api invoicing-portal --name production --expires-in-days 90
```

An application's token opens the A2A door only, on that one project. It starts and follows work; it
never takes a decision. See [A2A](../integrate/a2a.md).

### What can go wrong

| Message or symptom | What it means |
| :-- | :-- |
| **New project** is missing or refused | You are not an organisation admin |
| "Lowercase letters, digits and dashes only" | The identifier has another character in it |
| "The repository is not valid yet" | Write `owner/name` or an https address |
| A readiness line stays to do after you fixed it | Press **Test** on the connector: readiness reads the last test |
| A person cannot approve a step | They lack the role (Developer or above) or the step's group |

### Go further

- [Connectors](connectors.md): connect the tracker, the repository and the other systems.
- [Workflows](workflows.md): the process the project follows.
- [Project settings and readiness](https://github.com/VargaFoundation/choregos/blob/v0.26.0/docs/usage.md#project-settings-and-readiness), in depth.

---

## Work items

A work item is one request moving through a workflow: an issue, a ticket, a request filed in Choregos.
This page shows how to start one, follow it, read what each step produced, and step in.

**What you will be able to do**

- Start a work item from your tracker, from the board or from the command line.
- Follow it on the board and on its own page, live or as a replay.
- Read a run: its cost, its evidence, what the agent did and what was refused.
- Pause, resume, stop, replay a stage or move a work item to another workflow.

### Before you start

- To read work items: any role on the project.
- To file, pause, stop or replay: **Developer** or above.

### Start a work item

#### From your tracker

On GitHub, GitLab or Jira, open the issue and add the **`agent-ready`** label. That label is the only
trigger; other labels (`feature`, `bug`) choose the workflow through the project's routing. If a
webhook is lost, a catch-up pass finds the labelled issues nobody saw, within about a minute.

#### From the board

1. Open the project, then **Board**, and press **New work item**.
2. Pick the **Workflow** (the project's routing chooses it when you leave the default), then fill in
   the **Title**, the **Description**, the **Size**, and the **Fields of the work item** the workflow
   asks for.
3. Optionally, set a **Budget in USD**. It can only tighten the workflow's own budget.
4. Press **Create and start**.

With GitHub, Jira or GitLab as the tracker, Choregos creates the issue there first, then follows it.
With Choregos as the tracker, it gives the work item its key itself.

#### From the command line

On a project whose tracker is Choregos itself:

```bash
choregos items create onboarding --title "Arrival of a data engineer on 3 March" --size M
choregos items create onboarding --title "Quarterly access review" --workflow access-review --field team=data
```

Work can also start on a schedule, from a webhook or from another system: see
[Triggers](../integrate/triggers.md) and [A2A](../integrate/a2a.md).

### Follow a work item

#### On the board

The **Board**'s columns are the workflow's states. A card shows the work item's key and title; open it for the rest. Columns with no work item are hidden; press **Show empty columns** to see
them.

The board on your tracker (GitHub Projects, Jira) follows Choregos, not the reverse: moving a card
there does not move the work item. Move it from the console.

#### On its page

Open a work item. From top to bottom:

| Card | What it shows |
| :-- | :-- |
